claims.text: A continuous, coherent Cr2O3 or Al2O3 surface layer governs oxidation resistance in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys.
A continuous, coherent protective oxide layer governs retention of material integrity during high-temperature oxidation.
The protective oxide layer limits inward oxygen ingress.
The protective oxide layer limits outward migration of metal ions.
Sufficient concentrations of Cr or Al promote formation of a protective oxide barrier.
Cr2O3 has a compact structure and provides superior oxidation resistance.
Multiprincipal-element alloys inherently exhibit sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion in multiprincipal-element alloys stabilizes the protective oxide scale.
Sluggish diffusion stabilizes the underlying alloy matrix and thereby maintains mechanical integrity under oxidative conditions.
Alloys containing more protective oxide-forming elements will develop a more compact and adherent oxide layer than otherwise comparable low-Cr or low-Al alloys.
Alloys containing more protective oxide-forming elements will oxidize more slowly than comparable alloys with reduced Cr or Al.
Alloys containing more protective oxide-forming elements will retain mechanical strength better after oxidation than comparable low-Cr or low-Al alloys.
Reduced Cr or Al levels will produce less-protective, porous oxides and accelerated degradation.
The proposed governing behavior applies from 700 °C to 1000 °C for exposures up to about 100 hours.
Outside the proposed temperature and time range, evaporation of volatile oxides may become dominant.
The threshold Cr or Al concentrations required for effective protective-scale formation have not been quantified.
The effects of minor elements and grain boundaries on scale adherence and oxidation resistance remain unresolved.
